newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition baulks at opposition tax demands.
newsitem.headline: German coalition baulks at opposition tax demands.

text.p: German government leaders baulked on Friday after opposition Social Democrat (SPD) leader Oskar Lafontaine made new conditions for supporting tax reforms at cross-party talks next week.

Topping Lafontaine's shopping list was a call for a cut in occupational insurance charges in July. He welcomed remarks by Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Thursday signalling readiness to compromise on the issue.

"At last!" Lafontaine told Friday's Bild daily. "German unification was financed above all through social security contributions by workers in both the east and the west. This unjust financing has cost hundreds of thousands of jobs."

These so-called labour overheads are the highest in Europe and are seen as a job-killer which has put 4.5 million Germans on the dole. High unemployment and slow growth are putting Bonn's bid to join European monetary union under pressure.

Cutting these jobs charges is one of five demands Lafontaine said Chancellor Helmut Kohl must approve in "a binding, fundamental decision" if face-to-face talks between the two restarting next Tuesday are to succeed.
The SPD's other demands are: the government must make it clear how much the tax reform will cost; entry-rate income tax must be cut; tax-free allowances and child benefits must rise.
Waigel, however, changed his tone on Friday, saying: "I have the impression that Lafontaine is purely interested in populism and playing to the crowd.".

Waigel, who has drawn up a package of 30 billion marks ($17.4 billion) in corporate and income tax cuts to take effect over the next two years, said Lafontaine's demands were a wrong signal which would do nothing to stimulate job-creating investment.
"We need the tax reforms for investment -- now," he said on the fringes of a meeting of his Christian Social Union (CSU) party in the Bavarian town of Fuerth.
Peter Hintze, general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), said the party would accept no preconditions.
"Oskar Lafontaine's creativity in dreaming up new obstacles to the great tax reform knows no bounds," Hintze said.
And Hermann Otto Solms of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats told the B.Z. newspaper's Saturday edition: "I suspect Oskar Lafontaine does not really want an agreement."

The cross-party talks resume next week after a hiatus to try to find a compromise which would avert a drawn-out battle in parliament, where Lafontaine's SPD can block tax measures through its upper house majority.
Despite the controversy, there appears to be greater scope for compromise than before the SPD walked out of earlier talks at the end of February in a row over coal subsidies.
Waigel repeated on Friday that a cut in social insurance charges could be offset by raising indirect taxation -- but that move should come after welfare reforms are complete.
Any cut in social security charges this summer would probably be neutral for revenue. Lafontaine said he favoured raising petrol taxes in an offsetting measure.
"We prefer an ecology tax reform. But we are also ready to look at the coalition's proposals," he told Bild.
The "godfather" of the coalition tax reform drive, Gunnar Uldall of the CDU, welcomed Lafontaine's remarks.
"Now that the Social Democrats have at last said something constructive, we are a bit closer to agreeing," he told German radio. ($ = 1.720 German Marks)
